name: Alpha-linolenic acid (plant omega-3)
short: Prostate cancer: observational studies conflict, some tie high intake or blood levels to higher risk; trial meta-analysis: may slightly raise risk. Trials: LDL rose; bleeding time longer (1 trial).
text: Concern about alpha-linolenic acid has centred on prostate cancer, and the observational evidence is inconsistent. A 2004 meta-analysis of 9 cohort and case-control studies found an increased risk of prostate cancer in men with a high intake or blood level of alpha-linolenic acid (combined relative risk 1.70) and called the association a concern that warrants further study; a 2009 meta-analysis of 16 observational studies found high intakes or tissue levels weakly associated with prostate cancer (relative risk 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.01 to 1.43); when the studies were examined by type or by decade of publication, only the 6 studies measuring blood or tissue levels showed a statistically significant association, and after adjustment for publication bias there was no association (0.96); the authors concluded that high intakes or high blood and adipose tissue levels may be associated with a small increased risk of prostate cancer, a conclusion they qualified because of heterogeneity across studies and the likelihood of publication bias. Later meta-analyses of dietary intake did not confirm an increased risk: one of 12 case-control and prospective studies found a positive but non-significant association (1.08) and failed to confirm a link, one of 5 prospective studies found a pooled relative risk of 0.97 and a weak protective association, and a 2015 dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies found dietary alpha-linolenic acid inversely associated with risk (a result dominated by a single study) and no significant association for blood levels. These are observational studies of diet or blood levels, which show associations rather than causes; in a meta-analysis of 47 randomised trials of polyunsaturated fats, increasing alpha-linolenic acid had little or no effect on cancer death and may slightly increase prostate cancer risk (relative risk 1.30, 95% confidence interval 0.72 to 2.32). In a meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials in 1,183 adults with overweight or obesity, supplementation with plant sources of alpha-linolenic acid significantly increased LDL cholesterol while lowering triglycerides, C-reactive protein and systolic blood pressure. In a 3-month placebo-controlled trial in 22 people with rheumatoid arthritis, with a linoleic acid preparation as the placebo, the group given alpha-linolenic acid (from flaxseed) showed an increased bleeding time; the abstract does not say whether this differed from the placebo group, and it does not mention bleeding events or blood-thinning medicines. A 2014 review stated that toxicological data are limited but no serious adverse effects have been reported. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
